verdict.reasoning: Patient reports swelling noticed about a week ago, left elbow, not painful, slightly warm, and feeling fluid-filled: "about a week ago", "It's not painful at all", "It's the left elbow", "it's slightly warm, and I kind of feel like it's a bit fluid inside".
Patient states timing as: "I just noticed this, like, about a week ago or something."
Patient says: "It's not painful at all. I feel fine" in reference to the elbow swelling.
Patient describes: "I kind of feel like it's a bit fluid inside."
Patient notes: "it's slightly warm" and doctor confirms: "Yes, it's a bit warmer."
When asked about injury: "Have you banged that elbow? Did you have any kind of injury?" patient replies: "No, not really. Not that I know of. I haven't noticed anything."
When asked if this happened before, patient says: "No, no, I haven't noticed that before. I don't have any, like, history of... seeing this. I don't remember at all."
On palpation, patient reports: "On the tip of the elbow? It's okay. Just like next to it, like where the swelling is? It's a bit..." indicating focal tenderness adjacent to the olecranon.
Patient explicitly distinguishes: "On the tip of the elbow? It's okay. Just like next to it... it's a bit..." meaning the tip itself is non-tender.
Patient history: "I think I have something like osteoarthritis" and when asked, "Has anyone ever told you that?" patient answers: "Yes, a few years ago." Earlier identifies the clinician as "A gp."
Medication history: "And do you, are you on any medication on a regular basis?" Patient: "No, no."
Allergy history: "Well, not really. You know, I'M allergic to. To peanuts. That's pretty much all I had to say about my medical history."
Drug allergies: "Are you allergic to any medication?" Patient: "No, not that I know of."

Family history question: "Has anyone in your family got any kind of rheumatology diseases like rheumatoid arthritis or lupus... ?" Patient: "in my family, I'm not sure." This is not a clear denial of rheumatoid arthritis; it is uncertainty, so claiming a denial is not supported.
Same family history response: "in my family, I'm not sure." The fact does not match this uncertainty and instead states a denial, so it is not supported.
Work: "And in terms of your job, do you do anything physical?" Patient: "Not really, no. I just, you know, sit at the desk."
Exercise: "I do, I do do some sports. I run regularly. Like two, three times a week."
General health: Doctor: "And you normally fit and well, mobile, active?" Patient: "... Yeah, no, I'm. I think I'm healthy."
Combines two supported elements: desk work ("I just, you know, sit at the desk") and running 2–3 times weekly ("I run regularly. Like two, three times a week").

The doctor performs a visual tele-exam but never explicitly states that visible swelling over the olecranon is seen; swelling is only described by the patient. No quote like "I can see swelling" appears.
Doctor notes: "Well, I noticed the skin was a bit dry on the tip of the elbow."
Doctor confirms warmth: "Is it hot compared to the surrounding skin...?" Patient: "It's a bit warm?" Doctor: "Yes, it's a bit warmer."
On self-palpation: "On the tip of the elbow? It's okay. Just like next to it, like where the swelling is? It's a bit..." indicating mild tenderness lateral/adjacent to the olecranon.

The doctor later says the joint does not look like septic arthritis and discusses that emergency features would include it becoming "very red"; current absence of such description supports no marked erythema being present.

Doctor's assessment: "This seems like what we call the bursitis... that's an inflammation of one of the fluid sacs around the joint." History indicates no trauma ("No, not really" to injury). Location and context imply olecranon bursitis of the left elbow.
Doctor says blood tests will "also check for things like gout as well." This indicates gout is being evaluated as a possible etiology.
Blood tests are to "check for inflammatory markers, infection, rheumatological antibodies. So we'll do a full screen"—this is explicitly to assess inflammatory etiologies.

Doctor states it does not currently look like septic arthritis but warns about signs and says that would require urgent assessment; also mentions checking for infection in blood tests. This reflects assessing/ruling out septic etiology.
Peanut allergy is mentioned ("I'm allergic to peanuts") but there is no statement characterizing it as "stable" or making it part of the formal assessment; this descriptor is added.
Doctor instructs: "I would take ibuprofen regularly... That's 400 milligrams, three times a day. And you should take that after food, not an empty stomach."
"If you get any heartburn, stop taking it." This corresponds to advising to stop if dyspepsia occurs.

Doctor: "get some blood tests done... check for inflammatory markers, infection, rheumatological antibodies... and also check for things like gout as well." While exact labels (FBC, ESR/CRP, urate) are not named, a full lab screen for these purposes is explicitly planned; listing standard components is a direct clinical inference, not new positive data beyond what is implied.

Timing and mode: "results will come back to us after about five, six days..." and "we can arrange a follow up appointment... doesn't have to be face to face... over the phone... over video... That's your call. But you contact us after you've had the blood test done, and we can review things then."

Safety-netting: "if the elbow was to become very red, very painful, and the redness was to spread or become more intense, then you need to get on the phone or have a video appointment with one of us as soon as possible because that would be an emergency that would require more immediate assessment, more immediate treatment."
